sections.title: Person and number: the endings show the subject

body.p: Greek has three persons, singular and plural. The ending changes for each:
The 3rd plural has two forms: **γράφουν** (standard) and **γράφουνε** (everyday speech). The 2nd plural is also the **polite form** for one person: **Τι γράφετε, κύριε;** "What are you writing, sir?"
The dictionary form of a Greek verb is the **1st person singular present**, not an infinitive (Modern Greek has no infinitive): **γράφω** "to write" is literally "I write".
**Είμαι** "be" has passive-type endings and only two tenses (present and past).

The future is **θα είμαι** and the subjunctive **να είμαι**. There is no perfect of είμαι: "I have been (a teacher)" is **ήμουν** or formal **έχω διατελέσει**; "I have been to Paris" is **έχω πάει στο Παρίσι**.
**Έχω** "have" is a regular first-conjugation verb in the present, with an irregular past **είχα**:

ex.en: We had a lot of work.

body.p: Έχω also builds the perfect tenses (see below) and appears in impersonal phrases: **έχει ήλιο** "it's sunny", **έχει κόσμο** "there are people".

check.why: Ήμασταν (or ήμαστε) is the past of είμαι.

body.p: Active verbs fall into two conjugations, decided by where the stress is in the 1st person singular.
**First conjugation (Α΄ συζυγία):** stress on the stem, ending **-ω**: **γράφω, διαβάζω, πίνω, μένω, δουλεύω**. Endings as in part 1.
**Second conjugation (Β΄ συζυγία):** stress on the ending, **-ώ / -άω**. It has two types:

**Type A** (vowel -α- in the endings): αγαπάω "love", ρωτάω "ask", μιλάω "speak", ξυπνάω "wake up", περνάω "pass", πεινάω "be hungry", διψάω "be thirsty", γελάω "laugh", κρατάω "hold", ξεχνάω "forget", πονάω "hurt", τραγουδάω "sing", απαντάω "answer", σταματάω "stop", συναντάω "meet". The forms with -ά- are everyday; the -ώ/-ού- forms are a little more formal. Both are correct.

**Type B** (vowel -ει-/-ου-): μπορώ "can", οδηγώ "drive", ζω "live", θεωρώ "consider", προσπαθώ "try", ευχαριστώ "thank", παρακαλώ "ask, please", τηλεφωνώ "phone", αργώ "be late", χρησιμοποιώ "use", αφαιρώ "remove", βοηθώ "help", ωφελώ "benefit".

**Contracted verbs** of the first conjugation have a vowel before -ω and shorten some endings: **λέω** (λες, λέει, λέμε, λέτε, λένε), **ακούω** (ακούς, ακούει, ακούμε, ακούτε, ακούν(ε)), **τρώω** (τρως, τρώει, τρώμε, τρώτε, τρώνε), **πάω** (πας, πάει, πάμε, πάτε, πάνε), **κλαίω, καίω, φταίω**.

Many verbs have **passive endings** in -μαι. Some are true passives ("I am seen"), many are reflexive ("I wash myself") and many simply have no active form (**έρχομαι** "come", **σκέφτομαι** "think"). The forms are the same in every case.

list: **-ομαι** belongs to first-conjugation verbs: γράφομαι, πλένομαι, ντύνομαι, κάθομαι "sit", σκέφτομαι "think", χρειάζομαι "need", γίνομαι "become", εύχομαι "wish", αισθάνομαι "feel", δέχομαι "accept", εργάζομαι "work", κουράζομαι "get tired".
**-άμαι** is a small group: **θυμάμαι** "remember", **κοιμάμαι** "sleep", **φοβάμαι** "be afraid", **λυπάμαι** "be sorry".
**-ιέμαι** is the passive of Type A verbs: αγαπάω → αγαπιέμαι, ρωτάω → ρωτιέμαι, κρατάω → κρατιέμαι.
**-ούμαι** is the passive of Type B verbs and of learned verbs: θεωρούμαι, εξαρτώμαι (εξαρτάται), απαιτούμαι.

body.p: The 1st plural moves its stress to **-όμαστε**, and **έρχεστε** has the colloquial variant **ερχόσαστε**.

ex.en: What's your name? (literally: how are you called?)

sections.title: The two stems: imperfective and perfective

body.p: Every verb has an **imperfective stem** (for ongoing, repeated or habitual actions) and a **perfective stem** (for single, complete actions). The present uses the imperfective stem; the simple past, the simple future and most subjunctives use the perfective stem.
**How the perfective stem is formed** in regular verbs, by the last consonant of the present stem:

body.tip: Verbs in **-ζω** split between -σ- and -ξ-: **διαβάζω → διάβασα** but **παίζω → έπαιξα**. There is no reliable rule, so learn each with its past.

check.why: A liquid verb: no σ, vowel change: θα μείνω, έμεινα.

body.p: The simple past uses the **perfective stem** and the past endings **-α, -ες, -ε, -αμε, -ατε, -αν(ε)**. In verbs whose stem would otherwise leave the stress too far forward, the past adds an **augment ε-** (explained below).

**The stress always falls on the third syllable from the end** in the past tenses. That is why the 1st and 2nd plural (which have an extra syllable) move the stress forward: **έγραψα → γράψαμε**, **διάβασα → διαβάσαμε**. The 3rd plural also has the form with -ανε, which keeps the stress like the plural: **γράψανε, διαβάσανε**.

ex.en: Where did you go in the summer?

check.why: Third syllable from the end: πληρώσαμε.
Perfective stem αγορασ- + -ε, stress on the third syllable from the end: αγόρασε.

sections.title: Irregular pasts you need every day

body.p: The most common verbs have irregular perfective stems. They are worth learning as a set, with the past and the dependent form (used after θα and να).

ex.el: Είδες την ταινία; Όχι, δεν την είδα.
ex.en: Did you see the film? No, I didn't see it.
I want to tell you something.

body.p: The **dependent forms** δω, πω, βρω, βγω, μπω, πιω are stressed on the ending in all persons: **να δεις, να πει, να βρούμε, να βγείτε, να πιουν**.

check.why: A single act uses the perfective dependent: να σε δω.
Irregular stem φυγ-: έφυγα, θα φύγω.

body.p: The imperfect uses the **imperfective stem** with the past endings and expresses ongoing, repeated or habitual action in the past ("I was writing, I used to write").
**Second-conjugation verbs** (both types) form the imperfect with **-ούσα**: **μιλούσα, ρωτούσα, οδηγούσα, ζούσα**. Type A verbs also have a colloquial form in **-αγα**: **αγάπαγα, ρώταγα, μίλαγα**.

**Passive-form verbs** have the endings **-όμουν, -όσουν, -όταν, -όμασταν, -όσασταν, -ονταν**: **σκεφτόμουν**, **θυμόμουν** (θυμάμαι), **κοιμόταν** (κοιμάμαι), **αγαπιόταν**, **θεωρούνταν** (θεωρούμαι, learned).

ex.el: Όταν ήμουν παιδί, έπαιζα στον δρόμο.
ex.en: When I was a child, I used to play in the street.
I was reading when the phone rang.

check.why: Second conjugation: -ούσα (colloquial also μίλαγα). Μίλησα is the simple past.

sections.title: The augment: when the past gets an extra ε-

body.p: In the past tenses the stress must fall on the **third syllable from the end**. When a verb has a one-syllable stem (γράφ-, πίν-, κάν-), there is no third syllable to stress in the singular, so Greek adds a stressed **ε-** in front: **έ-γραψα, έ-πινα, έ-κανα**. When the ending adds a syllable (1st and 2nd plural), the augment is not needed and disappears: **γράψαμε, πίναμε, κάναμε**.
Verbs whose stem already has two syllables or more do not need an augment: **διάβασα, αγόρασα, άνοιξα, ξύπνησα**.
**Irregular augments.** A few verbs augment with **η-** or change the vowel: **θέλω → ήθελα**, **ξέρω → ήξερα**, **πίνω → ήπια** (past), **είμαι → ήμουν**, **έχω → είχα**.

**Verbs with a prefix** put the augment after the prefix when the verb is learned or formal (the internal augment, explained at the end of this document): **παράγω → παρήγαγα**, **συμβαίνει → συνέβη**, **εκλέγω → εξέλεξα**. Everyday compounds just stress the prefix: **ξαναγράφω → ξανάγραψα**, **κατεβαίνω → κατέβηκα**.

check.why: The plural adds a syllable, so no augment: κάνατε.
Θέλω has the irregular augment η-: ήθελα. (Θέλησα exists, as the simple past "wanted, decided".)

sections.title: Future and subjunctive: θα and να with two stems

body.p: The **future** is **θα** + a verb form; the **subjunctive** is **να** (or ας) + the same forms. Both come in two aspects:

**The dependent form** (εξαρτημένος) is the perfective stem with the present endings: **γράψω, γράψεις, γράψει, γράψουμε, γράψετε, γράψουν(ε)**. It never stands alone: it always follows θα, να, ας, or a conjunction like όταν, αν, πριν, μόλις.

ex.en: I'll write to you tomorrow. (one act)
I'll write to you every day. (repeated)
If (s)he comes, I'll talk to him.

body.p: The **passive dependent form** has its own perfective stem with stressed endings **-ώ, -είς, -εί, -ούμε, -είτε, -ούν(ε)**: **θα γραφτεί** "it will be written", **να ντυθώ** "to get dressed", **θα κουραστείς** "you'll get tired", **να σηκωθούμε** "for us to get up".

ex.en: I have to get up early.

check.why: Μη φοβάσαι is general ("don't be afraid"), μη φοβηθείς refers to one occasion; both are correct Greek.

body.p: The imperative has a **continuous** form (from the imperfective stem: "keep doing, do regularly") and a **simple** form (from the perfective stem: "do it now, once"). It exists only in the 2nd person; other persons use **να** or **ας**.
**Irregular simple imperatives**, all very common:

**Passive-form imperatives** have **-ου** in the singular and **-είτε** in the plural: **ντύσου / ντυθείτε**, **σήκω / σηκωθείτε** "get up", **κοιμήσου / κοιμηθείτε**, **θυμήσου / θυμηθείτε**, **ετοιμάσου / ετοιμαστείτε**. The continuous passive imperative is rare and uses **να**: **να προσέχεις!**

**Negative commands** never use the imperative form: use **μη(ν) + subjunctive**: **Μη γράφεις!** "Don't write (stop writing)!", **Μη γράψεις τίποτα!** "Don't write anything!", **Μη φύγεις!** "Don't leave!"
The passive simple past has its own stem, ending in **-θ-** (or **-τ-** after σ, φ, χ), with the endings **-ηκα, -ηκες, -ηκε, -ήκαμε, -ήκατε, -ηκαν**.
The stem matches the active perfective stem, with **-σ- → -στ-/-θ-**, **-ψ- → -φτ-**, **-ξ- → -χτ-**:

Several passive verbs have irregular pasts: **χαίρομαι → χάρηκα**, **στέκομαι → στάθηκα**, **βρίσκομαι → βρέθηκα**, **φαίνομαι → φάνηκα**, **γίνομαι → έγινα**, **έρχομαι → ήρθα**, **κάθομαι → κάθισα**, **λέγομαι → λέχτηκα**, **παντρεύομαι → παντρεύτηκα**, **πλένομαι → πλύθηκα**.

ex.en: Pleased to meet you! (literally: I was very glad)
Where did you meet / end up?

check.why: Passive past 1st plural: κουραστήκαμε. (Κουραζόμασταν is the imperfect: "we used to get tired".)

body.p: The perfect tenses use **έχω** (in the right tense) + an unchanging form called the **απαρέμφατο**, which looks like the 3rd singular dependent form: **γράψει, διαβάσει, αγαπήσει, δει, πει, φάει, έρθει**.
**Passive perfect**: έχω + the passive απαρέμφατο in **-θεί / -τεί**: **έχει γραφτεί** "it has been written", **είχε ντυθεί** "she had got dressed", **έχουμε κουραστεί** "we've got tired".

ex.en: Have you ever been to Naxos?
When I arrived, they had left.

ex.el: Μέχρι τον Μάιο θα έχω τελειώσει.
ex.en: By May I will have finished.
I would have come, if I'd known.

body.p: **Resultative alternative**: έχω + passive participle in -μένο, agreeing with the object: **Τα έχω γραμμένα** "I have them written (down)", **Έχω κλεισμένο τραπέζι** "I've got a table booked".

check.why: Pluperfect: είχαν + φύγει (the απαρέμφατο never changes).

sections.title: Verbs with irregular or alternating stems

body.p: Beyond the everyday irregulars, many verbs show vowel changes or stem alternations. Patterns:

**Verbs that change completely** (suppletive): βλέπω / είδα, λέω / είπα, τρώω / έφαγα, έρχομαι / ήρθα, πάω / πήγα. The same stems appear in compounds: **ξαναβλέπω → ξαναείδα, θα ξαναδώ**; **ξαναλέω → ξαναείπα, θα ξαναπώ**.
Learned compounds of these verbs often use a regular stem instead: **προβλέπω → πρόβλεψα, θα προβλέψω**; **επιβλέπω → επέβλεψα**; **προλέγω → προείπα**.
Formal Greek uses many learned verbs with older endings, especially in the passive.
**Learned passives in -ώμαι / -ούμαι (Type A in -άω)**: they keep an **-ω-/-α-** in the endings.

Common: **εξαρτάται** "it depends", **απαιτείται** "is required", **θεωρείται** "is considered", **επιτρέπεται** "is permitted", **απαγορεύεται** "is forbidden", **πρόκειται** "it is a matter of, is about to", **αφορά** "concerns", **εννοείται** "goes without saying", **ζητείται** "is wanted", **διαπραγματεύομαι** "negotiate", **εκτιμάται** "is estimated", **κινούμαι** "move", **ασχολούμαι** "deal with".

ex.en: It goes without saying that I'll come.

body.p: **Old imperfect forms in -ετο / -ατο** survive in formal writing: **εθεωρείτο** "was considered", **εξηρτάτο** "depended", **επρόκειτο** "was about to, was a matter of". In everyday Greek: **θεωρούνταν, εξαρτιόταν**, but **επρόκειτο** remains the normal form.

ex.el: Επρόκειτο να φύγει, όταν τον πήραν τηλέφωνο.
ex.en: He was about to leave when they called him.

check.q: Past of πρόκειται (in "he was about to leave"):
check.why: The learned imperfect επρόκειτο is the normal form.

sections.title: The internal augment of learned compounds

body.p: Learned compound verbs (prefix + verb, inherited from Ancient or Katharevousa Greek) put the augment **between the prefix and the verb** in the simple past and imperfect, instead of stressing the prefix. The augment is **-ε-** after a consonant, and it changes the final vowel of the prefix.

The internal augment appears **only where the stress needs it**, that is, in forms with no extra syllable: **υπέβαλα, υπέβαλες, υπέβαλε, υπέβαλαν**, but **υποβάλαμε, υποβάλατε**. Some verbs allow both (**μετέφερα / μετάφερα**, **προέβλεψε / πρόβλεψε**); the internal augment sounds more formal.

ex.en: The party elected a new leader.

check.why: Past of συμβαίνει with internal augment: συνέβη.

body.p: Formal and literary Greek preserves verb forms from Ancient Greek, especially in fixed phrases, legal texts and headlines. You need to recognise them, not produce them freely.

title: The verb I: forms and conjugations
blurb: Person endings, the conjugations, the two stems, past tenses, augment, future, subjunctive, imperative and perfect forms.

intro.p: The verb is the centre of the Greek sentence. One verb form tells you **who** (person and number), **when** (past or non-past), **how the action is seen** (aspect: ongoing or as a whole), **which voice** (active or passive form) and **which mood** (statement, wish, command). Because the ending says who the subject is, Greek usually leaves out subject pronouns.

This first verb document is about **forms**: how to build every tense from two stems. The second (Το ρήμα Β΄) explains what the tenses and moods mean and when to use them; the third (Το ρήμα Γ΄) covers voice, the passive, and how verbs combine with objects. Together they cover the whole system.

The key idea that makes the system manageable: **every Greek verb has two stems**, an imperfective (continuous) stem and a perfective (simple) stem, and each has an active and a passive version. Know the stems, and the endings do the rest.
